utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes, and that's about it. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, Mr. Vanderpuye. We are, as you may have noticed, sitting without Judge Kwon today, who couldn't be with us for personal reasons. So we are sitting -- we will be resorting to Rule 15 bis, paragraph (A) and we are pursuant -- sitting pursuant to that provision. I understand there are some preliminaries that you would like to raise. I don't know exactly who. Then I have received the wrong information. I was informed that there were going to be some preliminaries. I mean, it could have been a misunderstanding, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We can always arrange that, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. But it was spoken too soon, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The usual suspects all rise to our feet. As I think everybody is aware, there was a sort of an emergency motion filed yesterday to add three exhibits to the Prosecution's 65 ter exhibit list with respect to one witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. In fact I was going to ask you when that witness is due, is expected to come over.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think, realistically, given the schedule, we're looking at, and after consultation with various of my colleagues, probably Tuesday or perhaps Wednesday, if the estimates continue to hold. I think we have substantial cross-examination estimated for the next witness, not -- not this current witness. And then we have another witness, Witness number 48, who will follow that witness and then we have Witness 49 who is the subject of this motion. One thing I did want to raise, and I thank the Chamber for giving me the opportunity now, is after speaking with my learned friends, particularly from the Gvero team, there was one correction I wanted to make to the motion about which I alerted the team yesterday, immediately upon its filing. It's a -- it's a question of fact, as represented in the motion pertaining to the presence of the Accused Gvero at a meeting in July 1995 with Generals Smith and Mladic. The motion represents that that meeting took place in Zepa itself; in fact, that is not the case. That meeting occurred in Mrkonjic Grad, and that is on the 31st of July, and I just wanted to make that clear that for that meeting General Gvero was not present in Zepa, that meeting took place elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And that is in relation to which --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is, Mr. President, in relation to Roman numerals, subparagraph (ii) under paragraph 2, page 1 of the Prosecution's filing yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were obviously not very pleased about this; however, my learned friend was good enough to ring Mr. Krgovic almost immediately and tell him of the mistake. In an ideal world, we would like the Prosecution to file a correction. However, I note that the motion itself is confidential. This has been dealt with in open session, and the Prosecution have made it plain that it's not suggested that my client had any such meeting in Zepa at the material time. And therefore, bearing in mind my learned friend's good grace, we accept the correction and invite the Chamber to take note of it. So far as the motion itself is concerned, speaking for myself, I have not yet seen all of this material. My learned friend has told me that a CD is being burnt and we will have it during the course of the morning. Realistically we need to view that before we make any submissions. However, having spoken to some of the other Defence counsel, there is going to be certainly some opposition to the addition of this exhibit, and we may well support that opposition. But at the moment I'd like to reserve the Gvero Defence's position, if I may, until we have reviewed the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You certainly may, Mr. Josse. Would you like to have the floor now, or shall we hear what Madam Fauveau has to say first? Is it always in relation to the same issue? Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, and in fact I am the source of the opposition to which my colleague was referring to. I'm not talking about the essence of these exhibits. I have seen them, but I do not recall it exactly, but the Prosecutor, however, is continuously forgetting to put some exhibits on the list. I believe that it is no longer a simple omission. I believe that this is something that the Defence -- that the Prosecution could have done a long time ago, but almost a year ago a 65 ter list was made, this exhibit was not put on the list, and in -- on the 15th of February the Prosecutor told us which witnesses were going to testify -- to testify in March, and they told us which exhibits would be presented, and those exhibits were not included. Now, three or four days before the witness is called to the bar we have to find, verify those exhibits, so I'm -- my opposition is not so much to the fact that he wishes to add these exhibits, but if that is the case I would like the Defence to be granted a month in order to be able to prepare adequately for the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be clear, these are materials which have been in the Defence's possession for in excess of a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what you state in the motion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have furnished the time ranges for these four clips, which is what this video material amounts to, four video clips totalling at most, 15 minutes of playing time. I would suspect that after proofing the witness, which we have not yet had an opportunity to do, that will be cut down to approximately 10 minutes. But I have provided the time training ranges for those clips to the 100th of a second, basically, for each of those clips. We are, as was represented a moment ago burning those clips or burning the videos themselves again on to CD, just so there is no confusion. With the time ranges I've given, it shouldn't take more than a second to find each and every one of these very, very brief video clips. So I think the preparation time in connection with that, in terms of viewing them, should be minimal. I have done everything I can to minimise the time loss with respect to these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Thayer. We will obviously need to come back to this on Monday when we resume and when that would also give you the opportunity to go deeper into the matter and think about it and us the opportunity to be able to discuss it with Judge Kwon, who would be back with us on Monday, hopefully. All right. With regard to the protective measures that are sought in relation to Witnesses 48 and 49, are there any -- are you in a position now to confirm whether there are any objections or not? Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, speaking on behalf of our team only, we have some misgiving about this particular application; however, the stance we are going to take is that we are ultimately neutral. We would invite the Trial Chamber to examine the application very carefully. So far as 49 is concerned, we have considerable amount of cross-examination for 49, and frankly, if this application is granted, will virtually all have to be in private session because of the nature of the job that he did at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think we will come back to this on Monday as well. And perhaps you would be kind enough on Monday to enlighten us on the misgivings that you have, because I think we will need to dispense with the usual time limit for filing responses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We would be grateful for some mature reflection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the other hand, if you stand up and tell us you have got misgivings, we would like to know what they are, especially since you are inviting us to give due weight to the motion and to any misgivings or objections that there might be. So we will come back to it on Monday, Monday morning. And we'll then be able -- we'll then be in a position to respond. But if possible, could I invite the other Defence teams, if you also have misgivings, if you wish to object to the granting of protective measures, could you kindly Monday morning come prepared? You don't need to file a formal response, but could you Monday morning, please, be prepared to let us know what your objections might be. All right. I thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further preliminary matters? None. Okay. So I think we can -- yes -- yeah, okay. I suppose you are standing, ready to continue your cross-examination? Or for some other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I just wanted to point out to an inconsistency in the transcript from the -- yesterday's hearing. Page 26 of the transcript, my question to the witness contained the expression "framing us up" when the witness spoke about a certain person from Milici, line 11 of the transcript. And then the same situation on page 56, line 25 was described with the word "planted," which gives a somewhat different context to the entire situation. So I want this to state -- I want to state this for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know what the procedure is, because even last week we had an occasion of receiving a memo from the CLSS correcting parts of the transcript. So I'm sure it will be taken in hand, Mr. Mrkic. And I'm -- I hope you're satisfied with this. I mean there is a procedure that is usually resorted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning to you. Good morning to you, sir. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will do our best today to possibly finish with your testimony, but I am not in a position to guarantee you that. It depends on how many more questions Mr. Mrkic has. Do you plan to finish your cross-examination shortly, Mr. Mrkic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Half an hour at the longest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Witness, just for formality's sake, but also because it is important, you are still testifying pursuant to the solemn declaration that you made at beginning of your testimony, that you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Mrkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the meeting that you had on the 14th with the two officers. This has to do with the machinery and equipment that they sought. You said that you called the director of the brick factory in relation to that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the brickworks at the time had the machinery available, the one that you allegedly needed for the officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said it in plural. As far as I know the brickworks had only one piece of machinery; ULT.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did they ask for another piece of equipment except for the one that you mentioned now, ULT?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Just that one. Or rather, I told them that they had that one piece, and they were satisfied with that answer. As far as I know, they didn't inquire whether there were more pieces of equipment. Actually, I did tell them that the utility company had another small piece of machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And what was their reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you what was their reaction when I mentioned the driver. I've described to you their reaction at the time, and there was no other reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: When I asked you about the reaction, I wasn't referring to that reaction. Rather, I wanted to know whether they showed any interest for getting this other piece of machinery from the utility company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they didn't, they weren't interested in it, because I didn't even call the director of the utility company, I only called the director of the brickworks, and based on that I concluded they were not interested in that small machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: You basically anticipated my next question. I was going to ask you about the director of the utility company. You did not call the director of the utility company, nor did anybody ask you to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me to call him, and I didn't call him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I would like now to turn to a different situation. Reading yesterday's transcript of your testimony, I concluded, and you may correct me if I'm wrong, that in the interview that you had with Mr. Ruez in 1998 you basically did not understand why you were summoned and what the topic of the interview with Mr. Ruez was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really tell you the extent of my understanding at the time. I knew why they called me, they called me about the events of July 1995. In that interview I was guided by Investigator Ruez. Whatever questions I understood, I gave them answers, and you can find them in the interview. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that it was your understanding that Mr. Ruez was interested in the events surrounding the fall of Srebrenica or the liberation of Srebrenica, and the events that followed thereafter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever he asked me, I gave him answers. Now, if you are asking me to go back 10 years, and to analyse how I experienced that, what my thoughts were, it's too difficult. I simply answered the questions to the best of my ability at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you answered my question or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why don't you repeat your question. I don't know what you are hinting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Well, my question was clear. Were you clear about the fact that Mr. Ruez was interested in the events concerning Srebrenica itself and events after Srebrenica? And by this I'm referring to all of the events and the questions of Mr. Ruez focusing on that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was clear it me that he was interested in the Srebrenica events. What else would he be interested in? And whatever he was interested in I helped him with, to the extent that I was able.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you answered Mr. Ruez's questions concerning the events after Srebrenica to the best of your recollection at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely to the best of my recollection, certainly not to the worst of my recollection. Whatever recollections I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Does this then mean that the events you described to Mr. Ruez and the answers you provided to Mr. Ruez's questions are basically those that you considered to be truthful at the time when you were interviewed by Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reading this interview now, I gain an impression that Mr. Ruez didn't put questions clearly to me and that based on my answers he perhaps was only superficially satisfied. Perhaps you're going to misinterpret my words now. I'm not a lawyer, so I speak as a layman. But he was the one in charge of the interview. If something was unclear, he could have put additional questions to me in order to get all the answers. Looking at the interview now, it seems to me that he was satisfied with my answers. There were no follow-up questions, no additional questions. I don't know if what I said just now is clear enough to you. There was an interview, I provided answers. And, in my view, Ruez was satisfied with my answers. Perhaps I didn't attribute enough weight to certain things at the time, but I am not accustomed to these kinds of things. I'm not a judge, not a lawyer, and at the time that was the first time that I had met with an investigator in my life. That was the first time that I gave an interview where I was nervous, a bit scared. He could have done a better job with that interview, the investigator, in case I wasn't clear enough in some segments. That was the first contact I had with any kind of investigation, court, and at the time I was 50-something years old, and I had no previous experience with investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Sir, I do not wish to abuse or misuse anything you say, I'm just trying to clarify some things that are not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we can clarify that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what we're trying to do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever was unclear then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put the question to you this way: How many times did you see Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just once. That time and never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: After that did you see any other investigators from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: From then onwards, when was the first time that you had any contact with any lawyer relating to any issues pertaining to Srebrenica? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Momir Nikolic's attorney came. I think his name was Londrovic. That was during the Nikolic case, when that was underway. And that lawyer, I think his name was Londrovic, he spoke with me in Bratunac. To the effect, would I agree to testify if necessary, in the Nikolic case, and I agreed. And we talked, however this didn't actually materialise. I didn't come to the Tribunal in relation to the Nikolic case. *Later I spoke to the attorney Karnavas, who was defending -- oh, is somebody telling me something? No. Anyway, I spoke with Mr. Karnavas later with the Blagojevic case, and that's when I came to the Tribunal to testify, in the Blagojevic case. These are the conversations that I recall with the lawyers and investigators from the first contact with Mr. Ruez to -- until today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Mrkic. We are taking care of the redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to confirm one thing before I move to Mr. Blagojevic's attorneys. Were you friends with Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "friends," well, maybe that's not quite appropriate; maybe good acquaintances, lived in the same town. I think that those terms were better, that we were good acquaintances, close acquaintances, and that we lived in the same town. Friends? Perhaps that would be a bit too far. We were a little bit less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Avoid unnecessary question being put later on, when you say, were you friends with Mr. Nikolic, there being many Nikolics, you are referring to Momir Nikolic, weren't you, Mr. Mrkic? And you, too, that's how you understood it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant Momir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] *Q. While preparing to testify as a Defence witness in the Blagojevic case, did you see Mr. Blagojevic's attorneys once or -- or on more occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On more occasions. I think that I saw Karnavas in Bratunac once, Suzana, his assistant. I -- from what I understood, I met with her twice in Bratunac, and then again with Karnavas here at The Hague when I came to testify, in his office in a house somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... redactions, but if you can spare us having to continue doing this all the time, we would appreciate it, both of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I making a mistake in something, Mr. President? What should I be paying attention to. I mean, it's unintentional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. I'm not blaming you for having done it deliberately. Yesterday, you will recall that we tried to redact from your evidence details about possible testimonies or statements earlier on. The idea being to try and eliminate from the transcript those -- that information that could disclose your identity. So please refrain from mentioning any cases by name, which you have appeared as a witness. And if you need to mention, then let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will try to do that, but the attorney is putting his questions in such a way that I cannot seem to avoid it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that. But Mr. Mrkic, I think, understands that as well. But his -- his job is a difficult one, and you will appreciate that. Yes, Mr. Mrkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of caution, Mr. President, I think we should move to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. And I will have less papers to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: We can speak openly now. When you talked about Mr. -- when you talked with Mr. Nikolic's lawyer, the lawyer of Mr. Momir Nikolic -- well, let me rephrase the question. According to what you know, was Mr. Momir Nikolic, at the relevant time, in Bratunac or in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. But I didn't really meet him. I know that he was there in the area, Bratunac, Srebrenica, the area of responsibility that was his, yes. I know that he was there at the time, but I didn't meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And was Mr. Blagojevic there in that area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the relevant period that we are talking about, the 11th to the 14th --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, the interpreters didn't catch your answer. Could you please repeat it? The question was, "And was Mr. Blagojevic there in that area of responsibility?" And you had started saying, "Well, in the relevant period that we are talking about, the 11th to the 14th of ..." Can you continue from there, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that period from the 11th to the 14th, Blagojevic was in the area of responsibility, but I did not meet him. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I would just like to confirm one thing, and that is, according to the documents that we have at our disposal, you mentioned Mr. Beara for the first time during the trial before this Tribunal of Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And you were a witness of the Defence at the time, you were called by Mr. Blagojevic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And you were cross-examined by the Prosecution of The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The Beara Defence has no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's revert to open session, please. I thank you, Mr. Mrkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Mrkic for your cross-examination. You are now going to be examined, from what I could guess, by Mr. Zivanovic, who is lead counsel for Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, in your testimony, amongst our things, you mentioned yesterday or maybe the day before yesterday, members who were obliged or subject to work duty. I know what work duty means, but since this is an international tribunal, many of us do not know exactly what that is, what this work duty is. So I would like to ask you to explain what that term means, "work duty."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I start?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as much as I'm able to, I will do my best. Work duty also is something that conscripts are subject to, as well as others subject to military duty. They are mobilised, but they are not actually in the army, they work in companies that have to continue with their production process. They have to continue working. These conscripts are sent to work in companies, enterprises, so that the company can continue to operate and contribute, since in wartime it is necessary to continue with production, it's important to continue with living, working. I hope that I have managed to explain to the best of my ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you have. I would just like you to clarify one more thing for us. Does that mean that someone who is summoned to work duty is duty-bound, under the law, to respond; it's not a voluntary thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that person is mobilised and the mobilisation is conducted by the secretariat for national defence, and the person is assigned to the army or to work duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also told us that you attended this meeting with representatives of the Muslims when leaving the Srebrenica enclave was discussed. I would like to ask you to clarify one thing. You said, amongst other things, that General Mladic offered to the Muslim population that they could stay in Srebrenica with the condition that the army should hand over their weapons. I would like to ask you the following: Can you please clarify if this referred to the Muslim army that had been in Srebrenica up until that time, because we heard that the 28th Division was there. Was the condition practically that only the civilian population remains and that no armed people, no army, remains? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I perhaps omitted saying that the commander of the Dutch Battalion of UNPROFOR and his deputy attended this meeting. And from what I can recall, General Mladic asked them to demilitarise Srebrenica, which implied that the Muslims should hand over, actually the Muslim army that was in Srebrenica should hand over their weapons, the army that had been there for the previous three years, for as long as that lasted. I'm not sure now if the General meant that they should hand over their weapons to the VRS or to the UNPROFOR battalion, I'm not sure about that, but that this request was made for demilitarisation, and for weapons to be handed over at this meeting, yes, I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also talked about the distribution of humanitarian aid, not humanitarian aid, but the essential food stuffs in Potocari; bread, juices and so on that was distributed to the population. My question is, did you notice that this distribution of this assistance was filmed by TV crews?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a camera, and a man with a camera, but I didn't pay attention to that. But I do remember that there was a person walking along the asphalt road in Potocari, and they were filming. I didn't really pay that much attention to it, but I do remember that there was a camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We had the opportunity here to hear an assertion or a claim that the assistance was distributed only for as long as the camera was taping. As soon as the camera stopped filming the assistance was not distributed anymore, and what had a been distributed until then was taken back. Can you please tell us if this is true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not accurate. Assistance was distributed continuously throughout the day and the following day. Because the people were in Potocari for two days. I really cannot tell you with certainty how much aid was given, and I agree that it was insufficient, that our capacities were not enough. But to the extent that we were able to, we did provide assistance. It had been sent from Ljubovija, from Zvornik, it's true that it wasn't sufficient, but it went on continuously for those two days. And, as you said, that there was a claim that this had been done only because of the camera, that is not accurate, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say the assistance was insufficient, does that mean that you practically gave what you were able to give, what you had? It was simply insufficient, because you didn't have more to give?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a person named Jahic. I would like to ask you something regarding the departure of that person from Potocari. Could you give us the approximate age of that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that person is perhaps up to five years older than me. At that time I was 48, and that person was perhaps 52 or 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did somebody want to detain that person, to remain there? Did somebody want to prevent that person from entering the bus with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood me. That person, Jahic, can we mention the name, the first name? Jahic Omo. He was on the bus in front of the municipal building. He was sitting somewhere in the middle of the bus. And he knocked on the window as I came out of the municipal building and approached the bus. He was constantly on the bus, inside the bus. He didn't go in and out -- or out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I was wrong about the last name. I think that there was somebody whom you helped to get on the bus with his wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You were wrong. The Jahic person was in Bratunac, in front of the municipal building on the 12th in the evening. And in Potocari it was during the day on the 12th -- oh, no, actually, you're right. Both of them are called Jahic, both the person in Potocari, Jahic Nijazija, and the person on the bus in Bratunac is Jahic too, yes. Both of them are Jahic. You're quite right. But you were not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for that. So can you tell me about the first person? What was the age of that person? *A. Well, he was up to 60, Jahic Nijazija, and he built, before the war, my house in Bratunac, my family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So when you were there, and when you helped that person get on the bus, let me ask you this: Were there somebody else who wanted to move him away, to separate him from his wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From that spot, which was some 200 metres away, I took them personally to the bus and I saw them board the bus and sit on the seat. Nobody tried to separate them, and then I turned around and went back and never saw the man again. But he sent me a message, he lives today in Central Bosnia in Vares. Or Breza.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw that in your evidence you were quite accurate and specific when it comes to dates, and the dates can be quite significant to us. Since these events were quite a long time ago, I would like to know how good your recollection is when it comes to the dates. *A. I'm quite specific when it comes to the dates because I testified in Blagojevic case, and three days ago when I came to the Tribunal I listened to my entire testimony in the Blagojevic case. I took notes as I was listening to that, and the Prosecutor has my notes, and you do. This has refreshed my memory concerning the dates, the fact that I listened to the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Blagojevic case you testified some eight years after the events?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have been busy redacting as you go along. But let's go into private session, please. And again redact this last part as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you finish with the Blagojevic case questions we will revert back to open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You testified in the Blagojevic case some eight years after the Srebrenica events, as far as I could gather. Tell me, please, at that time, how clear was your memory about the events? Not only about the events, but dates, more specifically.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps initially it wasn't completely accurate and specific, but later on, as I started talking about it, things came back to me and things started falling into place, and I think that the chronology of some events became quite clear when it comes to the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And as things started falling into place, as you described it, as the puzzle pieces were put together, did you receive any assistance from the lawyers that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We met in Bratunac and, you know, we would talk to the lawyers for 10 hours or 10.00, and then we would meet again in the afternoon, and then I would get together with the people who were with me at the time, and we would exchange views and debate whether it was then or then. And then some 15 days later, lawyers would come again. And then in the meantime I had talked to other people as well in order to put all the puzzle pieces together and get the chronology right. So it's not like my memory was so good that in one single day I was able to reconstruct everything and say this was on the 11th, no. It took some time to get all the puzzle pieces together. And, yes, I received assistance from the lawyers. For example, the Executive Board, as the president of the Executive Board, I had a diary and I would record things on certain dates, describing my activities on that day. So that helped me get puzzle pieces together too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we revert to open session now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's do that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this diary that you just mentioned? Did you give it to someone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. It's possible that I destroyed it. I don't remember whether I still have it. Perhaps it's still in my house, but I don't know for sure that I still have it. It wasn't a very important document. It wasn't a very important record book or a formal diary. It was just for my purposes, and I can't even tell you to which extent that assisted me in putting the puzzle pieces together. *I received more assistance from my associates, people from the command, the preparations for the Blagojevic case lasted for quite a while. I was in Bratunac, and I was able to get information and to get the information about dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So we can basically conclude that the dates you provided in the Blagojevic case, the previous case, emerged after all the consultations you had with different people, with Defence counsel and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It came from various sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Reading about your previous testimony, and also reading the notes that we were provided with, we saw that you wrote down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, again, if it's necessary, go into private session. I mean if you look at lines 15, 16 and -- not just you, even the witness, obviously, but he was answering your questions, and now line 19. Let's go into private session. And please try to conclude this series of questions on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- we are in private session -- On the Blagojevic case and the witness's testimony so that we can revert to open session. It's three redactions that I have to sign in the space of one breath. We are in private session now, yes. We will continue in private session for a while. In the meantime, prepare the redactions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So in the Blagojevic case, as I have said, you spoke about being invited to the meeting on the 14th of July in the SDS premises. You testified, and this is also written in the notes of yours that we were provided with, apparently you were summoned, you received notice to attend the meeting at about 10.00. Yesterday you said that the notice arrived at around 9.30. So would you please tell us whether 10.00 is correct or did you subsequently change it to 9.30?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I actually said it, but my intention was to say that it was between 9.30 and 10.00 that I received a telephone call from Mirna, the secretary, to come to the SDS premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So would you please tell me, what made you change the time? From 1995 you had various interviews, testimonies, meetings with the Prosecutor, and in all of them you said that the call came at 10.00. But yesterday you said that the call came at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why this is significant. I don't even know whether I had a watch on me. Perhaps I didn't even look at it. So I can't tell you whether it was at 9.30 or at 10.00. My intention was to say that it was in the morning hours, between 9.30 and 10.00. I'm not sure now whether I came to the SDS premises at 9.30 or at 9.45 or at 10.00, but it was at around that period of time. I can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: You say that you came to the SDS premises at 9.30 or at 9.45. And earlier you said that you received a phone call at 10.00. Perhaps this doesn't seem significant to you, but it actually can be.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most likely it is significant to you. I apologise. We're overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, apart from overlapping, I think we've covered this territory enough. Let's move to your next question and please us whether we will continue in private session or we will revert to open session. But he's answered this question more than three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think he answered. He actually provided a new answer now. Until now he was saying when he received a phone call. And now he said about the time when he went there, actually. So I don't think this is an answer he already gave so I would like to pursue this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just wanted to point out, maybe to my learned friend, and also the Court, the reference that Mr. Zivanovic is referring to in the prior transcript is at page 9230 at line 6, and, in fact, what the witness said was that sometime after that, at 9.30 or thereabouts, that he received the call. And I think that that sufficiently answers the question. And I also object to Defence counsel's characterisation of the testimony as definitively at 9.00 [sic] because the record doesn't reflect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case we are of the opinion that he has answered the question when he said 9.30 or 10.00, he meant any time in between. So let's -- let's move forward, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you are now going to be examined by Madam Nikolic who is appearing here for Drago Nikolic. I know that you are very attentive, Ms. Nikolic, so I'm going to rely completely on you to tell us when we need to go into private session. Thank you. And you, Witness, try to avoid mentioning anything substantive or material that could identify your identity, which we have been trying very hard to keep from the public. Although I am pretty sure that everyone knows exactly who is testifying here now. Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will put only one question to you in open session and then we will move into private session. How common is the last name of Nikolic in Bratunac and that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very common.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's do that. I hope you're not going to ask him to mention them all, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sir, on page 37 and 38 of yesterday's transcript you mentioned two persons, two directors of a farm; Jovan Nikolic and Dragan Nikolic. Dragan Nikolic that you spoke of never served as an officer in the Zvornik Brigade, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can move back into open session, sir, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move back into open session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you know Drago Nikolic, an officer of the Zvornik Brigade, in that period, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just by seeing him around. We never actually were introduced, we never met in person. I didn't know him, somebody pointed him out to me. But we didn't actually know each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So in that period you knew his face, you knew what he looked like, you would recognise him in the street if you had met him? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would recognise him. He looks a lot like his brother, whom I know very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So in all the meetings that you attended and when you went to Potocari, at the Bratunac meetings, you did not see Drago Nikolic anywhere in those days, an officer of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Nikolic. Mr. Lazarevic, who is appearing for Borovcanin will be cross-examining you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Same advisory to you. I mean, I know you are very attentive, so let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I hope that we will finish this testimony very soon. And I would just like to ask you to answer my questions as briefly as possible and I try to formulate my questions so that you can answer with a yes or a no. If you don't know something, please feel free to say so. If you don't remember, also feel free to say that. In that way we will complete the cross-examination as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours, can we move into private session for just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, immediately. We've never refused to go into private session. So let's go into private session straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony before this Tribunal, you spoke about the meeting in the Hotel Fontana on the 12th of July, 1995, which you yourself also attended. There is no dispute about that. Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understood what you said properly, and you said that General Mladic practically provided the opportunity for the Muslim delegation to decide if they wanted to stay in Srebrenica or to choose to be evacuated, and also to pick the place to which they could be evacuated or the direction in which they would be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If for a moment we go back to the previous meeting which you -- or just an encounter, I wouldn't call it a meeting, that you had with General Mladic, that same day at 8.00 in the morning, it was actually the same thing this you also suggested to General Mladic during that meeting. The meeting that preceded this meeting in the Fontana, namely that the Muslims should be asked what they wanted to do, and how the matter should be resolved? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I also understood from your testimony that representatives of the Muslims, the three people who were at the meeting in the Fontana Hotel, refused any possibility of staying in Srebrenica, that they insisted on being evacuated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that they just wanted to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] One more question, and then I believe that we will be able to move into open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the meeting at the Fontana Hotel, were you aware that the meeting was being filmed by a camera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw a camera and the person who was operating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I believe we can move into open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go into open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had the opportunity to hear the testimony of a member of DutchBat here who attended the Fontana meeting on the 12th in the morning, and who said that the tape that he looked at did not actually capture the entire meeting. Do you allow for the possibility that the whole meeting was not filmed, that there was some interruptions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the camera was recording. I don't know if it recorded the whole meeting or just some of it. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You also said in your testimony that the Fontana meeting, attended by Muslim representatives from Potocari, members of the Dutch Battalion, members of the VRS, the civilian authorities from Bratunac and the commissioner for civilian affairs from Srebrenica, I hope I didn't miss anyone out, but that's not so important. Practically there was an agreement reached that the Muslim civilians should be evacuated in the direction of Kladanj and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name of the other town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And the agreement was reached --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said Kladanj and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Tuzla, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The agreement was reached, that specific agreement, to evacuate the Muslim population, and it was practically reached by adopting the proposal of the Muslim representatives; what they asked for was actually agreed to, it was accepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely so, at their explicit request. There was no compromise about them staying. They were quite firm and decisive, that they just wanted to go. To go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would now like us to look at, just for a minute, and please pay attention to what will be said, to a part of the footage from the Hotel Fontana, or from the hotel in Bratunac, which we will now play for you, and we can look at it together. And I hope that we will have the opportunity to comment that's so. This is video marked V004458. And the time that should be shown starts from 01.50.39 to 01.51.04.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, after we've looked at this segment --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Maybe we should move into private session. I apologise. I apologise [Previous translation continues] ... I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact I'm waiting to see what's happening, because it's the same like when you asked for the private session, we couldn't -- we couldn't -- are you asking for private session again?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Same thing. I mean, we are not following you in your own language. So when you speak in English -- in your own language, we don't get it. And it doesn't show up in the transcript as well, so we don't know exactly what you're saying. So Mr. Lazarevic is asking for private session. We already are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is just to protect your identity, since you attended the meeting and that could be something that could reveal your identity. So this is why we're doing it. Now that we have looked at this footage, just now, does that perhaps remind you of some details about what the Dutch representatives agreed on at this meeting? Were you able to -- excuse me. Were you able to understand well what the DutchBat commander said to General Mladic at this meeting and which is recorded in this footage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say, the interpreter was a person that I knew, and he was sitting there next to the UNPROFOR commander, and General Mladic and partially between Mladic and I'm not sure if I would be able to interpret him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is the possibility that you didn't hear that part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But in any case, for the purpose of some other questions that have to do with the later period, you saw here that Colonel Karremans, the commander of the Dutch Battalion, told General Mladic that his ministry, the Dutch defence ministry, ordered him as the commander of the Dutch Battalion, to offer all possible assistance in the evacuation of the population. You heard that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I heard that before as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And of course you heard that Colonel Karremans was offering General Mladic his battalion to help in the evacuation of the population. We just saw that a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was that offer. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now if we agree now, I think, about this, if we now advance in time forward into Potocari when you came to see the civilians, is what the commander said at the meeting and promised General Mladic was that actually implemented in practice and did the Dutch Battalion help in the evacuation of the civilians from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in Potocari itself was confusing. When I came to Potocari I saw soldiers of the Dutch Battalion in a cordon that was separating the population of Srebrenica from the road there. So that no one could approach them from the road. That was what I first saw, them standing about one or two metres apart from one another in a cordon that was some 30 or 40 metres long, so that they could stand between the population and the road so that somebody would just come there uninvited and so on. I mean, they were there, but that was, in my view, their main task, to separate the civilian population from other people who were in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You know, I don't want you to tell us something that you didn't see and that you did not experience yourself, so I will be happy to accept this answer of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And just to clarify something in the transcript, the video clip that we just saw is part of the trial video numbered P02047.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to make this clear, did you see yourself, recognise yourself in the video clip that we saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did. In the yellow shirt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I think we can move into open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Let's move into open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Witness, now we are in Potocari, and bread, water, and other articles are being distributed that the municipality of Bratunac managed to secure for the needs of the Muslim civilians there. During this distribution of bread and other food stuffs, juices, chocolates, was there ever a situation that the bread that had been distributed to the civilians already is taken back from them by the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no question of that. That is a preposterous -- well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that too, because there were some such indications, is it possible that once bread is distributed to the masses then it is taken back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this would not be possible, theoretically, and it wouldn't occur to anyone to do that at all. Just the idea of that is quite unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. During the time that you were in Potocari, you had the opportunity to meet some acquaintances, Muslims, let's not mention any names, to briefly chat with them. Was it your impression that those people that you were talking with, whom you knew, that you had a contact with at the time, was it your impression that they all wanted to go to Tuzla as soon as possible and leave Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. They all wanted to get on the buses out of turn, just so that they could leave Potocari as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you were able to see that with a large number of people there; in any case, I'm thinking of those civilians, Muslims who were in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of us who were there knew somebody, and we were all asked by someone for that kind assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Having that in view now, and the experience you had in Potocari, and what we talked about earlier about that certain agreement that had been reached, according to what you know did the representatives of Muslims who attended the Fontana meeting actually properly and accurately reflect the mood of the people, the civilians in Potocari whom they represented at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they did, but the Muslim representatives also were supposed to meet there with us, and they were supposed to distribute this aid, this humanitarian aid. However, we didn't see them up there. We didn't meet them in Potocari and we should have done so, they were supposed to be together with us. When we went up there nobody waited for us, so that we could hand over this aid to somebody in the sense that we had brought it and we were handing it over to somebody else to distribute. This did not happen. There was nobody there to wait for us and we didn't see anyone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So that was an agreement for the Muslim representatives to distribute the food. But they did not adhere to that, according to your information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. And then it was done, I don't even know how to describe it, but they were supposed to do that, and then we just did that without any kind of organisation or order. It was just done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's time for -- for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. We will continue with your cross-examination after the break, which will be of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And we can remain in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, just a couple of more questions and we will conclude with this cross-examination. While you were in Potocari during these events on the 12th and 13th of July, you had occasion to see members of the Dutch Battalion; you already testified about that, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And the members of the Dutch Battalion that you saw then were in their military equipment, they had helmets, flak jackets, weapons, all the proper stuff; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the period of time you stayed in Potocari, those two days, you did not observe any hostility, any hostile attitude of the Serb troops in relation to the members of the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see a single incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now for the end. Let me ask you this: You know Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: How long have you known him for, as best you can remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have known Borovcanin since 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What is your opinion of Mr. Borovcanin as a person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see Borovcanin as an honest man, good policeman, exceptionally educated man. Having such character traits, he was well respected in the place where he lived and worked. I could even say that he was very popular, which in my mind is not typical for a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you about his qualities, and I would like to reiterate that having such qualities and based on all the work that he had done, he was promoted to a rank of General.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. One moment, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, is it true to say that the civilian authorities were in function during the war in Bratunac, they were operational?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've mentioned, sir, yesterday, Dragoslav Trisic. Dragoslav Trisic, was an officer of the Bratunac Brigade and was he in charge of the liaison between the brigade and the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Trisic was a major and he was assistant commander for logistics. He was the person in charge of contact and coordination between the army and the municipal Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we say that a contact between the Bratunac Brigade and the municipal authorities of Bratunac were mainly limited to the supply of the brigade, the supplying of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. The contact was related to the logistics support of the municipality to the Bratunac Brigade in terms of providing food, clothing, cigarettes, those items mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And can we say that the command of the Bratunac Brigade was not involved in the daily life of the Bratunac -- of the city, in fact. I am talking about they were not interfering with the management of the city and how the city was being ran.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Executive Board, which consisted of seven members, one was an army representative, which is to say that six were civilians and one was a military man. So in that respect the army had some pool or some influence, because out of seven members of the Executive Board one was the army representative. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, but allow me to clarify. So the army had a representative of the Executive Board, but the brigade command did not usually call you to tell you what to do. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. As I said to you, Trisic, who was the assistant for logistics support, was the intermediary who conveyed their needs in terms of food, clothing, cigarettes, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On many occasions you mentioned Miroslav Deronjic. Is it right to say that at the time in 1995 Miroslav Deronjic was not only the SDS president of Bratunac, but he was also the president of the regional SDS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. Regional board of the SDS of the Birac region, which comprised Bratunac, Zvornik, Srebrenica, Sekovici, Milici, and Vlasenica municipalities. I think that I enumerated all of them. That was the Birac region. And Deronjic was the regional president of the SDS for that region.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we say that Miroslav Deronjic was a person that had a great influence on the events and life of the -- in the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In political sense, yes. He had influence. In the military sense, I don't think so, but in the political sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And, in fact, Miroslav Deronjic was very close to President Karadzic; he had personal dealings with Karadzic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the SDS Presidency. I think that the SDS leadership had seven vice-presidents. One of the seven was Deronjic, in my view, and Karadzic was the president of the SDS. So that's the top echelons of the political party.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And can we say that the relations between Deronjic and Ratko Mladic were not very good, that they had a conflictual relationship?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say so. There was no love lost between them, if one can say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we revert into open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me, in 1995 how many people lived in the city of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town of Bratunac, we didn't really have accurate records, but I would say 10 to 12.000. In the town itself. As for the municipality, perhaps another two to 3.000. Because there were parts near the Drina River that were populated. So I would say that the entire municipality of Bratunac had about 15.000 residents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And is it true to say that during the war there were a lot of refugees in the city of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the refugees from the Srebrenica municipality who were of Serb ethnicity moved into Bratunac. In my assessment, that amounted to some four to 5.000 of Serbs from the Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the civilian authorities in Bratunac, did they, before the event of the 11th of July, 1995, had any contacts with the DutchBat members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had. The Podrinje catering company from Bratunac, which ran the Fontana motel, supplied fresh fruit and vegetables and pastry to the Dutch Battalion. They would come at least three times a week, or rather the vehicle of the Dutch Battalion would come to the Fontana Hotel at least three times a week to take over fruit, vegetables, and pastry. That lasted for at least a year. They paid for the services to the catering company.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move back to private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You talked quite extensively on the meeting that took place on the 12th of July, 1995, at the Fontana Hotel, and you said a few times that General Mladic asked representatives if they wished to stay in the region or to leave. Is it right to say that at no time General Mladic suggested to the Muslim representatives that the Muslim population had to leave the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. The first option was always to stay, with all the guarantees that I enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you heard General Mladic talk during this meeting, is it right to say that you believed him at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed him. Sincerely believed him. Was convinced of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we say that at no time General Mladic threatened the Muslim representatives during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't threaten at all. He was quite clear. He said clearly, and that wasn't a threat, that those who had bloodied their hands in relation to the Serb people, would be prosecuted. Everybody else who had a clean past would have full freedom of movement, living, just like all other residents residing there without any type of discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And during that reunion, that meeting, General Mladic never used any unpleasant words towards the Muslim population, he was never insulting towards them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't. I think that he spoke very decently with full respect to all those present.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when the representatives of the Muslim population said that they wanted to leave, you believed this was really their will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true to say that the talks about the evacuation only began when it became clear that the Muslim population wanted to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can we go back into open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's revert to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about the humanitarian aid that was given to Potocari, and we will not go into that, but is it right to say that the medical staff of Bratunac went to Potocari to help the population that was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. An infirmary was established in Bratunac to treat sick Muslim residents. There were some 20 people staying there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You talked yesterday about a man, a handicapped man, and you said that you helped him get on the bus. Is it right to say that you helped personally about 30 people who were handicapped to get on the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I definitely helped a group of at least 30 disabled people in wheelchairs. I escorted them to a bus and helped them get on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you were helping these disabled people, General Mladic, was he there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was. I previously asked for the opinion of the General in relation to the disabled persons. Rather, I informed him that there were such persons, and that it would be a good idea to escort them to a bus in the first batch, and he approved of that and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were in Potocari you did not see any bodies, you did not see people who were killed in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you also did not see that men were separated from their families, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true to say that, in fact, you really didn't see a lot of able-bodied men in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And it seemed a bit peculiar to me. I could see elderly men, women, children there. I asked a couple of people whom I knew about some younger persons, inquiring about their whereabouts. They evaded answering. They said, "Well, they're somewhere around here, milling about." That's the kind of an answer they gave me. It only became clear later that they were actually not there at all, that they had gone towards the forest.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But in any case, during the period during which you were in Potocari, the men who were there were able to get on the buses themselves, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It was mostly the people that I described; the sick, the elderly, and so on. There were men of some 50 years old, but in good shape, and women in all age groups from young girls to grandmothers, 70 and 80 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've already stated that the people who were gathered in Potocari wanted to leave. Is it right to say that no one, and you knew a few of these people, no one told you that they wanted to stay in that region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when these people would get on the buses they went on the buses of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what, the buses were some 200 metres away from where the main crowd stood, and they were lined up towards the utility company, so perhaps the last buses were 300 to 400 metres away from the crowd. Thus groups were established. For example, if they -- there were five buses there at that point in time, then five groups of 50 people were established, and that's how they boarded. They had to do it in this way in order to avoid people stampeding. That was the only way to do. We prepared people to board buses that were all lined up.
